purpose: Five named-ocean informational features grounded in NOAA and National Oceanography Centre references; the global ocean remains continuous.
preservation: Editorial text only; no old location item added, renamed, or deleted and no purchasable item created.

records.name: Pacific Ocean
records.subtitle: The largest ocean basin

sections.title: An ocean on an enormous scale
sections.body: The Pacific reaches between the Americas and Asia and Oceania, stretching across much of Earth's surface. It is the largest and deepest named ocean basin, with enormous differences between warm equatorial water, temperate regions and cold northern and southern boundaries. Its size influences global weather and ocean circulation. A map centred on Europe can hide how much of the planet is occupied by this one connected marine space.

sections.title: Edges shaped by plates
sections.body: Deep trenches, volcanic islands and earthquake zones are associated with plate boundaries around much of the Pacific rim. The Mariana Trench contains the deepest known parts of the global ocean. Yet the ocean floor is not uniformly deep: underwater ridges, seamounts and broad plains create varied habitats and geological settings. Processes acting far below the waves help shape coasts and islands above them.

sections.title: Climate and living systems
sections.body: Trade winds, changing sea temperatures and currents influence conditions across the tropical Pacific. El Niño and La Niña are linked with changes in the coupled ocean-atmosphere system and can affect rainfall far from the basin itself. Coral reefs, coastal wetlands and deep ocean habitats support very different species. The productivity of a region depends on light, nutrients and water movement, not merely its latitude.

sections.title: Routes and connected communities
sections.body: Pacific island societies have sophisticated navigation traditions and long histories of movement and exchange. Modern trade, fisheries and scientific research depend on the ocean too. Pollution and changing climate conditions can travel or have effects across borders. The Pacific illustrates why the oceans are not empty spaces separating peoples: they connect communities and ecosystems on a planetary scale.

records.quickFact: The Pacific is Earth's largest and deepest ocean basin, but its habitats range from reefs to trenches.

records.name: Atlantic Ocean
records.subtitle: Currents linking continents

sections.title: A basin between continents
sections.body: The Atlantic lies between the Americas on one side and Europe and Africa on the other. Its northern and southern parts connect with neighbouring ocean regions, illustrating that a boundary on a map does not separate the water into isolated tanks. Coastlines, continental shelves and deep areas create a varied basin. Shipping routes and coastal settlements have long depended on the conditions found across it.

sections.title: Moving heat through water
sections.body: Surface winds and differences in temperature and salinity help drive a complex system of currents. The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation includes northward transport of relatively warm water and southward movement of colder deep water. This matters for climate, including parts of north-western Europe. It should not be confused with one simple river in the sea: the circulation has several components and varies across space and time.

sections.title: An ocean floor with a ridge
sections.body: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs through much of the basin, where tectonic plates move apart and new oceanic crust forms. Other areas include deep basins, continental margins and undersea mountains. Marine life occurs from coastal estuaries to deep-water habitats with almost no sunlight. Fish stocks and migration routes cross national jurisdictions, creating practical problems for management and scientific cooperation.

sections.title: History written across the sea
sections.body: The Atlantic has linked peoples through migration, exchange, exploration and trade, including the brutal transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans. Its history cannot be presented solely as a story of discovery from a European viewpoint. Today, shipping, fisheries and communications remain important, alongside challenges from warming, pollution and habitat loss. Studying the Atlantic requires attention to the water itself and to the societies connected by it.

records.quickFact: The Atlantic's overturning circulation is one part of the global movement of ocean heat.

records.name: Indian Ocean
records.subtitle: Monsoons and maritime connections

sections.title: Water bordered by three continents
sections.body: The Indian Ocean lies between Africa, Asia, Australia and the Southern Ocean. Its northern shores contain major bays, gulfs and seas, while tropical and subtropical waters extend over a broad basin. In many areas, coastal communities depend on fisheries and marine transport. The ocean's geography helps explain why routes across it connected distant ports long before modern ships and navigation systems developed.

sections.title: The seasonal influence of monsoons
sections.body: Winds change direction seasonally across parts of the northern Indian Ocean, associated with the South Asian monsoon system. These changes affect surface currents, rainfall and conditions for marine travel. They helped shape historic sailing patterns, although no one route or season could remove the risks of navigation. Ocean temperatures also influence atmosphere-ocean interactions that affect surrounding countries' weather.

sections.title: Reefs, currents and deep water
sections.body: The basin includes coral reefs, seagrass habitats, continental shelves, island environments and deep-ocean regions. Some waters receive nutrients from seasonal upwelling, supporting productive marine food chains. Elsewhere, warm water and changing environmental conditions place stress on sensitive ecosystems. The ocean's ecological differences can be better understood by following currents and coastlines than by treating it as a single tropical habitat.

sections.title: A shared history of exchange
sections.body: Ports around East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, South Asia and Southeast Asia were linked by maritime trade and cultural exchange. Merchants, sailors and communities moved languages, technologies and goods alongside their own histories and identities. Colonial expansion later changed many of those relationships through unequal power and forced labour. The Indian Ocean remains a connected region whose heritage involves many societies, not a single trading civilisation.

records.quickFact: The Indian Ocean's seasonal winds have influenced currents, rainfall and sailing routes.

records.name: Arctic Ocean
records.subtitle: Life beneath moving sea ice

sections.title: The smallest named ocean basin
sections.body: The Arctic Ocean occupies high northern latitudes, bordered by parts of North America, Greenland, northern Europe and Asia. It is the smallest of the five commonly recognised oceans, but it contains shelves, deep basins and large seasonal differences in ice cover. Winter and summer can produce radically different conditions. Its remoteness on a familiar world map should not obscure the communities and ecosystems linked to the region.

sections.title: Sea ice is habitat
sections.body: Sea ice forms from seawater and changes with seasons, currents and temperatures. Channels within it support microscopic life, while algae associated with ice provide food for organisms lower in the marine food web. Larger animals depend on these relationships through fish and other prey. Ice also reflects incoming sunlight, so changes to its area and thickness affect the surface energy balance.

sections.title: Changes in water and climate
sections.body: Warming air and water influence sea ice conditions, and fresh water from rivers or melting ice can change local salinity and density. These processes interact with ocean circulation and ecosystems. Scientists monitor ice using satellites, ships and other measurements rather than relying on one image of a summer or winter. Trends require records over many years and careful interpretation of regional differences.

sections.title: People and stewardship
sections.body: Indigenous peoples across the Arctic have extensive histories, knowledge and connections to marine environments. Their livelihoods and rights matter when discussing shipping, resource use and conservation. Changes in ice conditions can affect travel and food systems as well as wildlife. Describing the Arctic only through polar bears or melting ice would omit much of its human geography and the practical decisions communities face.

records.quickFact: Arctic sea ice supports food webs and affects how much sunlight the ocean reflects.

records.name: Southern Ocean
records.subtitle: The water surrounding Antarctica

sections.title: An ocean defined around a continent
sections.body: The Southern Ocean surrounds Antarctica and links with the southern parts of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific basins. Many maps show its northern boundary at 60 degrees south, although definitions have differed among organisations. This difference is worth acknowledging: the world's ocean is physically continuous, even when regions receive separate geographical names. Strong winds and large waves are characteristic of many Southern Ocean waters.

sections.title: A current circling the continent
sections.body: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows around Antarctica and connects major ocean basins. Its circulation influences the transfer of water, heat and nutrients across the Southern Hemisphere. Sea ice forms and melts seasonally around parts of the continent, changing the conditions available to marine life. The ocean and atmosphere interact closely here, making observations valuable for understanding the global climate system.

sections.title: Life in cold, productive waters
sections.body: Phytoplankton support food webs involving krill, fish, seabirds, seals and whales. Productivity varies with light, nutrients and sea ice, while changing environmental conditions can affect species differently. Antarctic ecosystems are not simply frozen deserts beneath water. Coastal, open-ocean and deep habitats have distinct ecological processes, many of which are difficult to study because of weather and remoteness.

sections.title: Science and international decisions
sections.body: Scientific expeditions use ships, buoys, satellites and other instruments to investigate currents and life in the Southern Ocean. International cooperation is important because water and wildlife cross jurisdictional boundaries. Protection involves difficult decisions about fisheries and climate pressures, as well as the practical challenges of working in remote environments. Studying this ocean reveals how strongly distant regions of the world can be connected through circulation.

records.quickFact: The Southern Ocean connects three major basins through currents circling Antarctica.
